extraction.name: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)
extraction.description: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) is a subset of 23 particularly challenging BIG-Bench tasks for which no prior language model result outperformed the average human-rater score. The benchmark includes 6,511 evaluation examples across 27 subtasks, focusing on tasks requiring multi-step reasoning, algorithmic reasoning, and natural language understanding.
extraction.creator: Mirac Suzgun, Nathan Scales, Nathanael Schärli, Sebastian Gehrmann, Yi Tay, Hyung Won Chung, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Quoc V. Le, Ed H. Chi, Denny Zhou, Jason Wei
extraction.citeAs: Mirac Suzgun, Nathan Scales, Nathanael Schärli, Sebastian Gehrmann, Yi Tay, Hyung Won Chung, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Quoc V. Le, Ed H. Chi, Denny Zhou, Jason Wei. Challenging BIG-Bench tasks and whether chain-of-thought can solve them. arXiv:2210.09261v1 [cs.CL] 17 Oct 2022.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was curated from the BIG-Bench benchmark by applying filtering criteria to identify challenging tasks. The filtering process involved selecting tasks with: more than 103 examples, human-rater baselines, multiple-choice or exact match evaluation metrics, and where the best reported model did not beat the average human-rater score. For all but three tasks in BBH, a random subset of 250 evaluation examples was taken.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data was sourced from BIG-Bench (Beyond the Imitation Game Benchmark), a collaborative benchmark with over 200 diverse text-based tasks. The original BIG-Bench data was collected through crowd-sourcing.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The preprocessing involved filtering BIG-Bench tasks based on multiple criteria: (1) filtering out tasks with more than three subtasks (209→187 tasks), (2) filtering out tasks with fewer than 103 examples (187→130 tasks), (3) filtering out tasks without human-rater baselines (130→85 tasks), (4) filtering out tasks that do not use multiple-choice or exact match as evaluation metric (85→78 tasks), (5) filtering out tasks where the best reported model beats average human-rater score (78→36 tasks), (6) filtering out extremely difficult tasks outside the scope of the work (36→23 tasks). For most tasks, a random subset of 250 evaluation examples was selected, with three examples reserved for few-shot prompting.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The original BIG-Bench tasks included human-rater annotations. Human raters were enlisted to manually solve each task and score them against golden labels to establish human-rater baselines. The human-evaluation component took almost a year, during which formatting and content of some tasks changed multiple times. Human-raters were allocated a few hours per day to solve a sub-sampled evaluation set and could use external resources such as the Internet.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper reports both average human-rater performance and maximum human-rater performance for each task. The authors acknowledge that human-rater scores are not fully representative of the entire population and express empirical difficulty of tasks. The human-rater performance varied significantly across tasks, with average scores ranging from approximately 25.7% to 94.4%.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The data, prompts, and Codex model outputs are all available at https://github.com/suzgunmirac/BIG-Bench-Hard
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper explicitly excluded the Moral Permissibility task, stating they did not want to delegate agency to models about moral judgement scenarios. The authors acknowledge that surpassing average human-rater performance should not be confused with true language understanding or reasoning.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The authors acknowledge several limitations: (1) Human-rater scores are not fully representative of the entire population, (2) The human-evaluation process had inconsistencies due to changes in task formatting and content over time, (3) Some task descriptions were hard to follow and could have been better-formulated, (4) Human-raters could use external resources, which may affect baseline comparability, (5) The results should be interpreted with care and surpassing average human-rater performance should not be confused with true language understanding or reasoning, (6) Some tasks were excluded as extremely difficult or requiring domain-specific knowledge (e.g., Checkmate in One requires chess expertise, Real or Fake Text has extremely long inputs).
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for evaluating language model capabilities on challenging reasoning tasks. The paper demonstrates two primary use cases: (1) Testing with standard answer-only prompting, and (2) Testing with chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. The benchmark is intended to measure capabilities and limitations of large language models on tasks believed to be beyond current model capabilities. The evaluation protocol uses greedy decoding with exact match accuracy as the metric.
